A Collective Bargain Notes Read after Confessions of a Union Buster . Interesting details on the L.A. Teachers' union . Specifically giving up pay for more green spaces for kids, combats arguments that teachers unions are greedy. Talks about how higher paid/skilled teachers are fired to avoid paying benefits and high turnover. Also talks about nursing. Some nurses being turned against each other by union busters. Also talks about the strategy of bringing in established unions and their representatives to start one's own union. Includes union busting tactics at the end of the book.

docs.text: Between Two Fires Notes I really enjoyed between two fires. I liked how the prose was readable but didn't feel too modern. I like that they kill the nice priest and then avoided the bury-your-gays trope by revealing his brother, who's both evil and significantly gayer. Recommended this book to a friend's dad, who didn't get through the first chapter because of the impending rape, which is frustrating because the rapists are all immediately gruesomely killed before they can do anything in the page after he quit. It's nice how averse he was to it, though.

docs.text: Confessions of a Union Buster Notes Super interesting book! Used as inspiration for a writing project. Some tactics he mentioned: Divide and Conquer: Highlight differences of interest between groups of workers. Men vs women, day shift vs night shift, young vs old, etc. Fixing some problems on behalf of management: Getting rid of core gripes to take steam away from the workers and make it clear that management is capable of solving problems without the union. Choosing mouthpieces from management: Since managers are barred from union membership, they can be held in specific anti-union training. Selecting for well-respected and senior staff, potentially dangling promotion or turning workers against each other. Walking the floor: One of the first steps, getting a feel for the office and pin-pointing popular workers and potential tensions. Captive Audience Meetings: Mandatory anti-union meetings for workers. Barrage of emails: Blowing union powers/information privileges to fear monger (EX: The union has a list of all of your emails and addresses!)

docs.text: Dangerous Games Notes The first half of Dangerous Games gives a history of roleplaying games and the Satanic Panic through its emergence in 1979-1982, its peak in 1982-1991, and its shifting focus amidst the super-predator craze of 1991-2001. The second half breaks down the purpose of play, reasons why the Christian Right fears imaginary worldbuilding, and how they engage in it anyway. It looks at religion as a roleplaying game and roleplaying games as religion. I was given this book for Christmas many years ago, but it sat on my desk. When I did a research project on Theophilus Riesinger , the priest who performed the infamous 1928 Earling Exorcism , I found references to a secret 1934 primary account that had been banned from publication by the Catholic Church. There were two original copies locked away in university libraries that weren't available online. I discovered a book chapter covering the document on an academic journals website and saw the author allowed PDF requests. I emailed him in a haze at 3 in the morning and only afterwards, when checking his website, did I realize he was Joseph Laycock, author of Dangerous Games. The book was sitting right in front of me on my desk at the time, unread. The next morning, Laycock emailed me back with a a 34-page PDF of his original scans of the lost texts from the university libraries- way more than I bargained for! This incident is why Joseph Laycock is my favorite author ever and also my best friend. Source Bugs's Bookshelf

docs.text: Debt: The First 5,000 Years Notes I was a big fan of The Dawn of Everything and wanted to read more David Graeber. This book spawned a fascination with wanting to plan a DnD setting and campaign focused around Debt. I really enjoy the individual anthropological case studies about how different cultures interact with Debt. I have a bunch of old notes I want to dig up and paste on this page. Specifically, the anecdote about the IMF and Malaria really hooked me from the beginning and made me question my belief in the truthism that People ought to repay their debts . This book motivated me to read Margaret Attwood's Payback . I feel like it also made me think about Homewreckers in a new light.

docs.text: Evil Geniuses Kurt Andersen (2020) Central argument Beginning in the 1970s, wealthy business interests, conservative intellectuals, and political organizations coordinated a decades-long effort to reverse the economic policies established under the New Deal . Through think tanks, lobbying, legal networks, and electoral politics, they weakened labor unions, reduced taxes on the wealthy, deregulated industries, and expanded corporate power. The Reagan Revolution institutionalized these changes, while subsequent Democratic administrations preserved many of them. Andersen argues that rising inequality and economic insecurity were not inevitable consequences of globalization or technology, but substantially resulted from political decisions. Mechanisms and evidence 1. Organizing the conservative counterrevolution In 1971, corporate lawyer Lewis Powell wrote the Powell Memorandum for the U.S. Chamber of Commerce , urging businesses to organize against regulation and criticism of capitalism through universities, media, courts, and political advocacy. The Heritage Foundation (1973), American Enterprise Institute , and Cato Institute developed free-market policy proposals and cultivated political influence. Milton Friedman and Friedrich Hayek supplied intellectual arguments against government intervention. Economic stagnation and inflation during the 1970s increased their influence. 2. Reagan's economic transformation Ronald Reagan 's Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 reduced the highest marginal federal income-tax rate from 70% to 50%. Further legislation reduced it to 28% by 1988. During the 1981 PATCO Strike , Reagan fired more than 11,000 striking air traffic controllers, signaling reduced federal support for organized labor. Reagan appointed business-friendly regulators and pursued weaker enforcement of environmental, labor, and economic regulations. Supply-Side Economics promised that tax reductions would stimulate investment and growth. Andersen argues that the resulting benefits disproportionately accrued to high-income households. 3. Reshaping courts and competition policy The Federalist Society , founded in 1982, developed conservative legal networks that influenced judicial appointments and constitutional interpretation. Robert Bork and the Law and Economics movement promoted antitrust standards emphasizing consumer prices and efficiency rather than corporate concentration itself. This narrower interpretation of Antitrust Law helped make corporate mergers and consolidation more acceptable, even when they increased the economic power of large firms. 4. Financialization and shareholder primacy Milton Friedman 's 1970 argument that corporations should prioritize shareholder returns became increasingly influential in corporate management. Stock-based executive compensation rewarded managers for increasing share prices, encouraging restructuring, layoffs, and financial engineering. Leveraged Buyouts allowed investors to purchase companies using borrowed money, often leaving acquired businesses responsible for substantial debt. In 1982, the Securities and Exchange Commission adopted Rule 10b-18, providing a safe harbor for certain corporate stock buybacks. Repurchases subsequently became an increasingly important use of corporate funds. 5. Weakening workers and transferring risk Globalization and automation weakened manufacturing employment, but Andersen argues that American labor policies amplified their effects. Declining Labor Unions reduced workers' bargaining power, contributing to a growing separation between productivity gains and wage growth. The shift from defined-benefit pensions toward 401(k) retirement plans transferred investment and retirement risks from employers to employees. Employment-dependent health insurance and weaker job security increased the personal consequences of unemployment. 6. Bipartisan acceptance of neoliberal economics Jimmy Carter supported deregulation before Reagan, including the Airline Deregulation Act of 1978 , demonstrating that market-oriented reforms crossed party lines. The Democratic Leadership Council encouraged Democrats to embrace market competition, fiscal restraint, and business-friendly policies. Bill Clinton supported NAFTA , implemented in 1994, and signed the Gramm–Leach–Bliley Act (1999), removing important barriers between commercial banking, investment banking, and insurance. Andersen argues that Democratic acceptance of these policies helped make the conservative economic transformation durable. 7. Corporate influence and political obstruction Conservative organizations and corporate donors financed policy research, lobbying, legal advocacy, and political campaigns to defend favorable economic arrangements. Fossil-fuel interests supported campaigns opposing climate regulation, including efforts to undermine public acceptance of climate science. Citizens United v. FEC (2010) expanded protections for independent political expenditures by corporations and other organizations. Andersen argues that concentrated economic wealth increasingly translated into political influence, making reforms threatening established business interests harder to enact. 8. Inequality and the failure of trickle-down promises After 1980, income and wealth gains became increasingly concentrated among high earners, executives, and owners of financial assets. Andersen argues that reductions in top tax rates, weaker unions, financialization, and shareholder-centered management contributed to this distribution. Other wealthy capitalist countries maintained stronger labor protections and social insurance despite experiencing similar technological and global economic pressures. The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 reduced the corporate income-tax rate from 35% to 21%, continuing a central objective of the conservative economic movement under Donald Trump .

docs.text: Except for Palestine Marc Lamont Hill and Mitchell Plitnick (2021) Central argument American progressives frequently defend civil rights, self-determination, and international law while making exceptions for Israeli policies toward Palestinians. Bipartisan military assistance, diplomatic protection, and restrictions on political boycotts have helped sustain Israeli control over Palestinian territory. These contradictions predate Donald Trump and persist within the Democratic Party. Mechanisms and evidence 1. Recognition and Palestinian statehood In 1975, Henry Kissinger committed the United States to withholding recognition of the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) until it recognized Israel and accepted UN Resolutions 242 and 338. The PLO recognized Israel in 1988. Under the 1993 Oslo Accords , Israel recognized the PLO as the Palestinian representative but did not recognize Palestinian statehood. Benjamin Netanyahu subsequently emphasized recognition of Israel specifically as a Jewish state, complicating Palestinian claims to equality and refugee return. The authors argue that recognition requirements imposed obligations on Palestinians without equivalent Israeli commitments to sovereignty. 2. Zionism and Palestinian rights Zionism sought Jewish national self-determination in Palestine, where Palestinian Arabs also held national and territorial claims. Ze'ev Jabotinsky argued in The Iron Wall (1923) that Jewish state-building required military superiority because Palestinians would resist displacement. The Nakba displaced hundreds of thousands of Palestinians in 1948. Their property claims and Palestinian Right of Return remain unresolved. The authors question whether maintaining a Jewish demographic majority can be reconciled with equal Palestinian rights. 3. BDS and free speech Palestinian organizations launched Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) in 2005, demanding an end to occupation, equal citizenship, and refugee rights. The movement followed the 2004 International Court of Justice opinion finding Israel's separation barrier in occupied territory contrary to international law. Numerous American states passed anti-BDS laws restricting public contracts with boycott participants. NAACP v. Claiborne Hardware Co. (1982) established constitutional protections for political boycotts. Federal courts blocked several anti-BDS restrictions. The authors distinguish criticism of Israeli policies from Antisemitism , arguing that accusations of prejudice can be used to suppress legitimate political opposition. 4. Trump's policies and bipartisan precedents Israel captured the Golan Heights in 1967 and extended its laws there in 1981. UN Security Council Resolution 497 rejected the annexation. Trump recognized Israeli sovereignty in 2019. The Jerusalem Embassy Act (1995) directed relocation of the American embassy. Clinton, Bush, and Obama postponed implementation; Trump moved it in 2018. In 2018, Trump ended American funding for UNRWA , which provides education, health care, and assistance to Palestinian refugees. The authors argue that Trump expanded longstanding American support for Israeli territorial claims rather than creating that support independently. 5. Gaza disengagement and blockade Under Ariel Sharon , Israel removed settlements and permanent ground forces from Gaza in 2005 but retained substantial control over borders, airspace, and maritime access. Hamas won the 2006 Palestinian legislative elections. The United States imposed diplomatic and financial pressure while supporting rival Fatah forces associated with Mahmoud Abbas and Mohammed Dahlan . Hamas seized control of Gaza following armed conflict with Fatah in 2007. Israel and Egypt subsequently restricted Gaza's movement and trade. Restrictions, military destruction, and political division contributed to unemployment, infrastructure deterioration, and humanitarian dependency. The authors argue that disengagement reduced Israel's administrative responsibilities without establishing Palestinian sovereignty. 6. Military operations and accountability Operation Cast Lead (2008–2009) caused extensive destruction in Gaza. The Goldstone Report investigated alleged violations by Israeli forces and Palestinian armed groups. Operation Protective Edge (2014) produced further civilian casualties and infrastructure destruction. During the Great March of Return (2018), Israeli forces shot Palestinian demonstrators near Gaza's separation barrier. The authors argue that American diplomatic protection and military assistance reduced pressure for accountability despite repeated civilian casualties. 7. Progressive political opposition Bernie Sanders criticized Israeli military actions during the 2016 Democratic presidential primaries. Rashida Tlaib and Ilhan Omar entered Congress in 2019 and publicly defended Palestinian rights. The authors identify growing Democratic support for criticizing settlements and conditioning assistance, while congressional leadership remained reluctant to impose consequences. Historical alternative Under the Egypt–Israel Peace Treaty (1979), Israel agreed to withdraw from the Sinai Peninsula in exchange for peace and security arrangements. Withdrawal was completed in 1982. The authors contrast this negotiated withdrawal with continued Israeli control of the Golan Heights and Palestinian territories. Arguments challenged Palestinians refuse to recognize Israel: The PLO recognized Israel in 1988 without obtaining Palestinian statehood. BDS is inherently antisemitic: Criticism of Israeli state policy is not automatically hostility toward Jews. Anti-BDS laws protect against discrimination: Government contracting restrictions can penalize constitutionally protected political activity. Trump alone transformed American policy: Several policies had bipartisan precedents. Israel ended its occupation of Gaza in 2005: Israel retained substantial external control. Hamas alone caused Gaza's crisis: External restrictions, American intervention, and Palestinian factional conflict also contributed. American progressives consistently defend human rights: The authors identify exceptions involving Palestinian sovereignty, civilian protection, and political expression. Further questions What explains bipartisan American support for Israel despite disagreements over settlements and Palestinian statehood? docs.title: Except for Palestine

docs.text: American progressives frequently defend civil rights, self-determination, and international law while making exceptions for Israeli policies toward Palestinians. Bipartisan military assistance, diplomatic protection, and restrictions on political boycotts have helped sustain Israeli control over Palestinian territory. These contradictions predate Donald Trump and persist within the Democratic Party.
docs.title: Central argument

docs.text: In 1975, Henry Kissinger committed the United States to withholding recognition of the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) until it recognized Israel and accepted UN Resolutions 242 and 338. The PLO recognized Israel in 1988. Under the 1993 Oslo Accords , Israel recognized the PLO as the Palestinian representative but did not recognize Palestinian statehood. Benjamin Netanyahu subsequently emphasized recognition of Israel specifically as a Jewish state, complicating Palestinian claims to equality and refugee return. The authors argue that recognition requirements imposed obligations on Palestinians without equivalent Israeli commitments to sovereignty.
docs.title: 1. Recognition and Palestinian statehood

docs.text: Zionism sought Jewish national self-determination in Palestine, where Palestinian Arabs also held national and territorial claims. Ze'ev Jabotinsky argued in The Iron Wall (1923) that Jewish state-building required military superiority because Palestinians would resist displacement. The Nakba displaced hundreds of thousands of Palestinians in 1948. Their property claims and Palestinian Right of Return remain unresolved. The authors question whether maintaining a Jewish demographic majority can be reconciled with equal Palestinian rights.
docs.title: 2. Zionism and Palestinian rights

docs.text: Palestinian organizations launched Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) in 2005, demanding an end to occupation, equal citizenship, and refugee rights. The movement followed the 2004 International Court of Justice opinion finding Israel's separation barrier in occupied territory contrary to international law. Numerous American states passed anti-BDS laws restricting public contracts with boycott participants. NAACP v. Claiborne Hardware Co. (1982) established constitutional protections for political boycotts. Federal courts blocked several anti-BDS restrictions. The authors distinguish criticism of Israeli policies from Antisemitism , arguing that accusations of prejudice can be used to suppress legitimate political opposition.
docs.title: 3. BDS and free speech

docs.text: Israel captured the Golan Heights in 1967 and extended its laws there in 1981. UN Security Council Resolution 497 rejected the annexation. Trump recognized Israeli sovereignty in 2019. The Jerusalem Embassy Act (1995) directed relocation of the American embassy. Clinton, Bush, and Obama postponed implementation; Trump moved it in 2018. In 2018, Trump ended American funding for UNRWA , which provides education, health care, and assistance to Palestinian refugees. The authors argue that Trump expanded longstanding American support for Israeli territorial claims rather than creating that support independently.
docs.title: 4. Trump's policies and bipartisan precedents

docs.text: Under Ariel Sharon , Israel removed settlements and permanent ground forces from Gaza in 2005 but retained substantial control over borders, airspace, and maritime access. Hamas won the 2006 Palestinian legislative elections. The United States imposed diplomatic and financial pressure while supporting rival Fatah forces associated with Mahmoud Abbas and Mohammed Dahlan . Hamas seized control of Gaza following armed conflict with Fatah in 2007. Israel and Egypt subsequently restricted Gaza's movement and trade. Restrictions, military destruction, and political division contributed to unemployment, infrastructure deterioration, and humanitarian dependency. The authors argue that disengagement reduced Israel's administrative responsibilities without establishing Palestinian sovereignty.
docs.title: 5. Gaza disengagement and blockade

docs.text: Operation Cast Lead (2008–2009) caused extensive destruction in Gaza. The Goldstone Report investigated alleged violations by Israeli forces and Palestinian armed groups. Operation Protective Edge (2014) produced further civilian casualties and infrastructure destruction. During the Great March of Return (2018), Israeli forces shot Palestinian demonstrators near Gaza's separation barrier. The authors argue that American diplomatic protection and military assistance reduced pressure for accountability despite repeated civilian casualties.
docs.title: 6. Military operations and accountability

docs.text: Bernie Sanders criticized Israeli military actions during the 2016 Democratic presidential primaries. Rashida Tlaib and Ilhan Omar entered Congress in 2019 and publicly defended Palestinian rights. The authors identify growing Democratic support for criticizing settlements and conditioning assistance, while congressional leadership remained reluctant to impose consequences.
docs.title: 7. Progressive political opposition

docs.text: Under the Egypt–Israel Peace Treaty (1979), Israel agreed to withdraw from the Sinai Peninsula in exchange for peace and security arrangements. Withdrawal was completed in 1982. The authors contrast this negotiated withdrawal with continued Israeli control of the Golan Heights and Palestinian territories.
docs.title: Historical alternative

docs.text: Palestinians refuse to recognize Israel: The PLO recognized Israel in 1988 without obtaining Palestinian statehood. BDS is inherently antisemitic: Criticism of Israeli state policy is not automatically hostility toward Jews. Anti-BDS laws protect against discrimination: Government contracting restrictions can penalize constitutionally protected political activity. Trump alone transformed American policy: Several policies had bipartisan precedents. Israel ended its occupation of Gaza in 2005: Israel retained substantial external control. Hamas alone caused Gaza's crisis: External restrictions, American intervention, and Palestinian factional conflict also contributed. American progressives consistently defend human rights: The authors identify exceptions involving Palestinian sovereignty, civilian protection, and political expression.

docs.text: Homewreckers Aaron Glantz (2019) Central argument The 2008 Financial Crisis transferred housing wealth from homeowners to banks and institutional investors. Government bank rescues, foreclosure practices, discounted asset sales, and unequal access to financing helped investors acquire distressed properties while millions lost their homes. Several beneficiaries later gained political influence under Donald Trump . Mechanisms and evidence 1. Government-backed bank acquisitions IndyMac collapsed in July 2008. The FDIC sold its banking operations to investors led by Steve Mnuchin in 2009, creating OneWest Bank . The FDIC Loss-Sharing Agreement required the government to absorb portions of qualifying mortgage losses, reducing investors' exposure. The arrangement also covered qualifying loan modifications. Sheila Bair , FDIC chair, advocated modifications to prevent unnecessary foreclosures. 2. Foreclosure practices OneWest Bank and its subsidiary Financial Freedom faced criticism over aggressive foreclosures, including reverse mortgages. Reverse Mortgages could trigger foreclosure following a borrower's death, departure from the home, or failure to pay taxes and insurance. Robo-Signing and servicing errors allowed foreclosures to proceed using inadequately verified documents. Sandy Jolley investigated OneWest's foreclosure practices after her family's experience. 3. Institutional acquisition of housing Blackstone , led by Stephen Schwarzman , established Invitation Homes and purchased tens of thousands of houses after the crash. Institutional investors used access to capital, cash purchases, and foreclosure auctions to acquire properties at a scale unavailable to most households. Tom Barrack 's Colony Capital also acquired distressed housing through corporate entities that obscured ultimate ownership. Houses previously owned by families became rental properties, transferring future appreciation and rental income to investors. 4. Unequal access to financial relief Banks could sell foreclosed properties at discounts substantially below former owners' mortgage balances, while homeowners often struggled to obtain comparable principal reductions. Government programs including TARP stabilized financial institutions; HAMP offered mortgage assistance but depended heavily on lenders and servicers. Glantz questions why public intervention more effectively protected financial assets than existing homeownership. 5. Financialization of rental housing Invitation Homes helped develop Single-Family Rental Securitization , using rental portfolios and their expected income to support securities sold to investors. Wall Street could finance and profit from rent payments rather than solely from homeowners' mortgage payments. Large landlords gained access to additional capital for acquiring properties. 6. Racial disparities Redlining and discriminatory mortgage lending restricted Black and Latino households' access to affordable credit and homeownership. Predatory and high-cost lending increased exposure to foreclosure. The loss of home equity compounded existing racial wealth disparities. 7. Political influence Steve Mnuchin became Treasury Secretary; Wilbur Ross became Commerce Secretary; Stephen Schwarzman chaired Trump's Strategic and Policy Forum; Tom Barrack chaired his inaugural committee. Fred Trump had previously built substantial real-estate wealth with government housing assistance. Glantz connects government-supported property accumulation with the political influence of wealthy investors. Historical alternative The Home Owners' Loan Corporation (1933) purchased and refinanced distressed mortgages to prevent foreclosures. Glantz contrasts this direct intervention with the post-2008 emphasis on financial stabilization and investor acquisitions. New Deal housing policy also reinforced racial discrimination. Arguments challenged Irresponsible borrowers caused the crisis: Risky lending, servicing practices, and financial incentives also contributed. Foreclosure was unavoidable: Mortgage modifications and principal reductions offered alternatives in some cases. Bank rescues benefited everyone equally: Financial institutions received protections that did not necessarily preserve household ownership. Corporate landlords simply restored housing markets: Their purchases also concentrated ownership and redirected appreciation and rental income. Real-estate fortunes were purely self-made: Public guarantees, subsidies, and financial rescues helped create opportunities for private accumulation. Further questions Did the FDIC's loss-sharing terms make foreclosure financially preferable to modification in particular cases? Why could investors purchase distressed properties at discounts unavailable to existing homeowners? How much institutional housing consolidation resulted from government policy versus market conditions? Which specific policies resulted from the political influence of the investors Glantz profiles?

docs.text: The Chickenshit Club Jesse Eisinger (2017) Central argument The Department of Justice gradually abandoned aggressive prosecution of corporate executives, particularly after the 2008 Financial Crisis . Following successful prosecutions in the Enron scandal, corporate lobbying, unfavorable court decisions, and increasingly cautious DOJ leadership weakened the government's willingness and ability to bring complex financial fraud cases to trial. Instead of prosecuting individuals, the government increasingly negotiated settlements with corporations, collecting large fines without establishing individual criminal responsibility. Eisinger argues that prosecutors became more concerned with avoiding courtroom losses than testing potentially criminal conduct before juries. Mechanisms and evidence 1. Enron and the decline of aggressive prosecution The Enron Task Force , led initially by Leslie Caldwell , prosecuted executives following Enron's 2001 collapse. Prosecutors Kathy Ruemmler and Sean Berkowitz helped build cases against Kenneth Lay and Jeffrey Skilling , demonstrating that complex executive fraud could be prosecuted. Accounting firm Arthur Andersen was convicted of obstruction of justice in 2002 over document destruction connected to Enron. Its collapse, followed by the Supreme Court's 2005 reversal of the conviction, became a warning against indicting major corporations. Corporate defense attorneys used the Andersen case to argue that prosecution could destroy businesses and harm innocent employees. The DOJ increasingly favored negotiated settlements. 2. The origins of corporate settlements In the 1970s, Stanley Sporkin at the Securities and Exchange Commission investigated corporate bribery and secret slush funds. These investigations helped produce the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act of 1977. In 1994, US attorney Mary Jo White 's office developed an early Deferred Prosecution Agreement (DPA), allowing a company to avoid prosecution by accepting conditions. In 2003, PNC Financial Services received a DPA after using sham transactions arranged by AIG Financial Products to move troubled assets off its balance sheet. AIG Financial Products reached its own agreement in 2004, paying over $126 million. DPAs became a standard alternative to corporate indictments, allowing prosecutors to announce enforcement victories without proving charges at trial. 3. Corporate resistance to prosecution The 2003 Thompson Memorandum encouraged prosecutors to consider corporate cooperation, including access to privileged information, when deciding whether to indict. In the KPMG tax shelter investigation, prosecutors pressured the firm over its payment of employees' legal fees. Judge Lewis Kaplan ruled that the government had violated defendants' rights, resulting in the dismissal of major charges. Corporate lobbying and defense attorneys pushed back against DOJ demands for attorney-client privilege waivers. The 2006 McNulty Memorandum restricted prosecutors' ability to demand such waivers. The Supreme Court's 2010 ruling in Skilling v. United States narrowed the federal honest-services fraud statute. The Obama administration sought only a limited legislative repair, excluding private-sector corruption. 4. The revolving door and institutional incentives Covington & Burling exemplified the revolving door between corporate defense firms and government. Eric Holder worked at Covington before becoming Obama's attorney general and returned afterward. Lanny Breuer , Obama's criminal division chief, had also worked at Covington, representing major corporate clients. Corporate settlements offered prosecutors fines, publicity, and measurable victories without the expense or risk of trials. Defense firms could negotiate favorable resolutions while charging substantial legal fees. The growing salary gap between government prosecutors and corporate defense lawyers encouraged experienced attorneys to leave public service. 5. Failed prosecutions after the financial crisis After Lehman Brothers collapsed in September 2008, investigators examined its use of Repo 105 transactions to temporarily remove liabilities from its balance sheet. Neither Lehman executives nor auditor Ernst & Young faced criminal charges. The SEC investigated Goldman Sachs 's Abacus mortgage deal, in which hedge fund manager John Paulson helped select assets while betting against them. Goldman settled civil charges for $550 million in 2010 without admitting wrongdoing. Former Goldman trader Fabrice Tourre was found civilly liable in 2013. Senior executives were not charged. Prosecutors investigated accounting and valuation practices at AIG Financial Products , including conduct involving Joseph Cassano , but brought no criminal charges against its executives. 6. Prosecutorial caution and abandoned investigations Prosecutor Paul Pelletier spent years investigating AIG-related accounting transactions. His efforts encountered resistance within the DOJ, including under criminal division leadership. Lanny Breuer emphasized the potentially devastating consequences of criminal charges against major financial institutions, reinforcing caution about corporate prosecutions. Investigations involving Countrywide Financial , Washington Mutual , Citigroup , Bank of America , and other financial institutions ended without criminal indictments of senior executives for financial-crisis misconduct. Eisinger argues that prosecutors increasingly treated difficulty proving a case as a reason not to bring it, rather than allowing juries to evaluate contested evidence. 7. Judicial challenges to settlements In 2009, Judge Jed Rakoff challenged a $33 million SEC settlement with Bank of America over disclosures concerning bonuses at Merrill Lynch . He questioned whether the agreement adequately established responsibility. In 2011, Rakoff rejected a $285 million SEC settlement with Citigroup over misleading mortgage securities, criticizing the absence of admitted facts. The Second Circuit overturned Rakoff's rejection in 2014, limiting judicial authority to scrutinize SEC settlements. Rakoff continued criticizing the government's failure to prosecute senior financial executives, disputing DOJ arguments that sophisticated investors made fraud cases too difficult to prove.

Instead of prosecuting individuals, the government increasingly negotiated settlements with corporations, collecting large fines without establishing individual criminal responsibility. Eisinger argues that prosecutors became more concerned with avoiding courtroom losses than testing potentially criminal conduct before juries.

docs.text: The Divide Matt Taibbi (2014) Central argument American criminal justice operates under two increasingly unequal systems. Poor people, particularly racial minorities and immigrants, face aggressive policing, surveillance, and punishment for minor offenses, while wealthy individuals and corporations frequently resolve serious financial misconduct through civil settlements without criminal prosecution. Taibbi argues that this divide reflects institutional choices rather than simply differences in criminal behavior. Financial regulators increasingly negotiate with powerful institutions, while police, immigration authorities, and welfare agencies expand enforcement against vulnerable populations. The result is a system in which poverty invites scrutiny and wealth provides protection from it. Mechanisms and evidence 1. Selective prosecution after the financial crisis In 2012, Manhattan District Attorney Cyrus Vance Jr. charged Abacus Federal Savings Bank , a small Chinese American bank, and several employees with mortgage fraud. The bank had reported suspected employee misconduct and its mortgages had continued performing. Major institutions including Bank of America , Citigroup , and JPMorgan Chase faced multibillion-dollar settlements over defective mortgages without comparable corporate criminal trials. Taibbi contrasts the prosecution of Abacus with regulators' reluctance to prosecute systemically important financial institutions, whose collapse was considered a potential economic threat. 2. HSBC money laundering and marijuana arrests In 2012, HSBC agreed to pay approximately $1.9 billion after investigations uncovered failures to prevent money laundering involving Mexican drug cartels and transactions connected to sanctioned countries. The Department of Justice , under Criminal Division chief Lanny Breuer , negotiated a deferred prosecution agreement rather than pursuing a corporate conviction, citing possible consequences for the financial system. In New York, Tory Marone , a homeless man, was arrested after police found marijuana during a search. Although New York had decriminalized possession of small amounts, displaying marijuana in public remained punishable, creating opportunities for arrests following police searches. Taibbi contrasts the treatment of minor drug possession with the settlement offered to a bank that had facilitated enormous illicit financial flows. 3. Broken-windows policing and criminal records Andrew Brown , a Brooklyn resident with a criminal history, repeatedly encountered aggressive police scrutiny despite efforts to rebuild his life. New York's Broken Windows Policing strategy prioritized minor offenses and public-order violations, disproportionately exposing residents of heavily policed neighborhoods to searches and arrests. Minor arrests could generate court appearances, legal expenses, lost employment, and criminal records even when charges were dismissed. Taibbi contrasts this enforcement with corporate misconduct cases, where negotiated settlements often avoided comparable individual consequences. 4. Lehman Brothers and financial opacity Before its 2008 collapse, Lehman Brothers used Repo 105 transactions to temporarily remove tens of billions of dollars in assets from its balance sheet, making its leverage appear lower during reporting periods. After Lehman's bankruptcy, Barclays acquired substantial parts of its American operations through an emergency sale whose valuation and disclosure practices generated litigation. Complex transactions, private negotiations, and limited transparency made financial misconduct difficult to investigate and prosecute. Taibbi argues that financial complexity effectively shields powerful institutions from scrutiny routinely imposed on ordinary defendants. 5. Immigration enforcement as routine policing Section 287(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act allowed participating local law enforcement agencies to perform federal immigration enforcement functions. In Gainesville, Georgia, undocumented workers faced detention and potential deportation following routine police encounters, including traffic stops. Georgia immigration restrictions and driver's-license requirements made ordinary transportation dangerous for undocumented residents, encouraging reliance on Latino-owned taxi services. Immigration proceedings operated through an administrative court system with fewer procedural protections than ordinary criminal courts. Even minor encounters could lead to detention and family separation. 6. Hedge funds and the Fairfax campaign Hedge funds betting against Fairfax Financial Holdings sought to undermine confidence in the Canadian insurer and its CEO, Prem Watsa . Spyro Contogouris participated in a campaign involving hostile communications, allegations of financial wrongdoing, and efforts to influence journalists and investigators. Short sellers could profit from falling share prices while using negative publicity and financial research to intensify pressure on targeted companies. Taibbi examines how wealthy financial actors could mobilize sophisticated campaigns against opponents without attracting the kind of policing applied to street-level misconduct. 7. Welfare surveillance and unequal fraud enforcement In California, welfare recipient Maria Espinosa experienced an intrusive home inspection after applying for public assistance. Welfare fraud investigations could involve unannounced visits, searches of personal belongings, and scrutiny of household relationships. Riverside County's welfare fraud enforcement program pursued suspected misrepresentations by benefit applicants, including relatively small financial discrepancies. Taibbi contrasts aggressive investigations of poor recipients with large corporate fraud settlements that frequently imposed no individual criminal penalties. 8. JPMorgan Chase and consumer debt After acquiring Washington Mutual in 2008, JPMorgan Chase pursued collections on large portfolios of consumer debt. Former Chase employee Linda Almonte alleged that the bank relied on inaccurate records, defective affidavits, and improper debt-collection practices. She lost her job after raising concerns. Chase obtained judgments against thousands of credit-card borrowers through a legal process in which many defendants lacked the resources to challenge documentation. Taibbi contrasts the severe consequences imposed on indebted consumers with the limited personal accountability of executives overseeing defective collection systems. 9. Expanding enforcement against ordinary citizens In 2011, musician Patrick Jewell was arrested in Brooklyn following a police encounter over a cigarette. His case was eventually adjourned in contemplation of dismissal. Taibbi contrasts routine street arrests with financial regulators' treatment of influential Wall Street figures, including the Securities and Exchange Commission investigation involving John Mack and investigator Gary Aguirre . Aguirre alleged that senior SEC officials obstructed his investigation of suspected insider trading involving powerful financial executives. The book identifies a recurring institutional pattern: ordinary citizens face immediate coercive enforcement, while wealthy suspects often benefit from negotiation, political influence, and regulatory discretion.

docs.text: The Hundred Years' War on Palestine Rashid Khalidi (2020) Central argument The Israeli–Palestinian conflict is a century-long struggle shaped by settler colonialism and foreign intervention, rather than a symmetrical conflict between two national movements. British imperial policy, followed by American military and diplomatic support, enabled Zionist state-building, Palestinian displacement, and Israeli territorial expansion. Khalidi identifies six major assaults on Palestinian national rights between 1917 and 2014. He also criticizes Palestinian leadership for factionalism, failed diplomacy, and strategically counterproductive violence. Mechanisms and evidence 1. British sponsorship of Zionism (1917–1939) In 1899, Yusuf Diya al-Din al-Khalidi warned Theodor Herzl that establishing Jewish sovereignty in Palestine would threaten its existing inhabitants. Herzl responded by emphasizing the economic benefits of Jewish immigration. The 1917 Balfour Declaration endorsed a Jewish national home while recognizing Palestinians only as non-Jewish communities with civil and religious rights, not national rights. Under the British Mandate for Palestine , the Jewish Agency received official recognition and developed political, economic, and military institutions without a Palestinian equivalent. Britain violently suppressed the 1936–1939 Arab Revolt , weakening Palestinian leadership and armed resistance before 1948. 2. Partition and the Nakba (1947–1949) The United Nations Partition Plan for Palestine allocated approximately 55% of Palestine to a proposed Jewish state, although Jews constituted roughly one-third of the population. During the Nakba , approximately 700,000–750,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled. Zionist and Israeli forces depopulated hundreds of villages, including through forced expulsions at Lydda and Ramle . Israel prevented most refugees from returning. Property confiscation, including under the 1950 Absentees' Property Law , consolidated wartime displacement into permanent dispossession. 3. Occupation and settlement expansion (1967–1979) The Six-Day War brought the West Bank, East Jerusalem, and Gaza under Israeli occupation. UN Security Council Resolution 242 addressed Palestinians primarily as refugees rather than a people entitled to sovereignty. Israeli governments established settlements, roads, and security infrastructure in occupied territory. The Allon Plan proposed retaining strategically important areas, particularly the Jordan Valley. The Camp David Accords secured peace between Egypt and Israel without Palestinian sovereignty. Proposed Palestinian autonomy left fundamental territorial and political questions unresolved. 4. Destruction of the PLO in Lebanon (1982) Ariel Sharon directed Israel's invasion of Lebanon, seeking to eliminate the Palestine Liberation Organization 's military and political presence and establish a friendly Lebanese government. Israel besieged Beirut, forcing the PLO leadership into exile in Tunis. During the Sabra and Shatila Massacre , Israeli-allied Lebanese militias killed Palestinian and Lebanese civilians. Israel controlled the surrounding area; the Kahan Commission found Sharon personally responsible for failing to prevent the massacre. 5. The First Intifada and Oslo (1987–1995) The First Intifada mobilized Palestinians through strikes, boycotts, demonstrations, and local committees, shifting resistance toward popular participation. The Oslo Accords established the Palestinian Authority but postponed sovereignty, borders, Jerusalem, refugees, and settlements. Under Oslo II, the West Bank was divided into Areas A, B, and C. Palestinian authorities administered limited areas while Israel retained extensive territorial and security control. Khalidi argues that Oslo effectively subcontracted aspects of occupation to Palestinian institutions without granting them sovereignty. Settlement expansion continued throughout negotiations. 6. The Second Intifada and Gaza (2000–2014) The Second Intifada followed the failure of the 2000 Camp David negotiations. Khalidi criticizes Palestinian suicide bombings for killing civilians, undermining international support, and strengthening Israeli military retaliation. Hamas won the 2006 Palestinian legislative election. Western pressure and violent rivalry with Fatah contributed to the 2007 division between Hamas-controlled Gaza and the Fatah-dominated West Bank. Israel's Blockade of the Gaza Strip , alongside Egyptian border restrictions, severely constrained movement, trade, and reconstruction. Israeli military operations in 2008–2009, 2012, and 2014 caused extensive civilian casualties and infrastructure destruction. Khalidi connects these operations to the Dahiya Doctrine of overwhelming military force. 7. American diplomatic protection The United States replaced Britain as Israel's principal external sponsor through military assistance, diplomatic protection, and mediation. Khalidi argues that American negotiations repeatedly prioritized Israeli security while postponing Palestinian sovereignty. The Obama Administration opposed settlement expansion rhetorically but did not impose meaningful consequences. Khalidi contrasts this with Obama's willingness to confront political opposition over the Iran nuclear agreement. Conclusion Khalidi argues that Palestinian dispossession has been maintained through military force, unequal diplomatic recognition, settlement policy, and international sponsorship. Palestinian political fragmentation and failed strategies have compounded these disadvantages. He advocates unified Palestinian representation, international solidarity, engagement with Israeli society, and a political settlement based on equal rights rather than indefinite occupation or limited autonomy.

docs.text: The Israel Lobby and U.S. Foreign Policy Notes This is one of the books I have been most frustrated about my lack-of-specific-recall for. I have gone back through summaries to try and log what I feel is most important. Part 1 The United States, Israel, and the Lobby Camp David Accords (1978) - Negotiated under Jimmy Carter between Menachem Begin and Anwar Sedat. Israel and Egypt peace. US Support for Israel goes further than for other countries Israel: Strategic Asset or Liability? During Cold War , Israel allied with America against Soviet-backed Arab states Six-Day War (1967) Israel defeated Egyptian, Syrian, Jordinian forces Occupied the West Bank, Gaza Strip, East Jerusalem, Sinai Peninsula, Golan Heights Demonstrated Israel's military power. Yom Kippur War (1973) Egypt and Syria attacked Israeli positions Richard Nixon authorized major American resupply operation 1973 Oil Embargo September 11 Attacks Al-Qaeda and Osama bin Laden - American support for Israel was one of many grievances invoked by Laden. A Dwindling Moral Cause Balfour Declaration (1917) - British statement supporting a national home for the Jewish people in Palestine British Mandate for Palestine - Period of British administration after World War I , during which tensions between Jewish and Arab communities intensified. UN Partition Plan (1947) - Proposed dividing British Mandatory Palestine into Jewish and Arab states. Nakba (1948) - Palestinian term meaning catastrophe, referring to the mass displacement and dispossession of Palestinians during the war surrounding Israel's creation. 1948 Arab-Israeli War - Another term for the Nakba . Israel established independence, approximately 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled. Narrative that "Palestinians voluntarily abandoned their homes" 1967 Occupation - What is the "Israel Lobby" ? AIPAC ADL "Anti-Defamation League" Christian Zionists Neoconservatives - America world police, align with hard-line pro-Israel stances The book stresses that PACS and Lobbying are a part of the American democratic system and that Pro-Israeli groups Lobbying politicians is not the concern. Rather, the degree of influence and the resulting policies. Dominating Public Discourse Think tanks - WINEP (Washington Institute for Near East Policy) - Produces Middle East Policy research - Brookings Institution - Think tank. Middle East policy research. - Alan Dershowitz - Harvard law professor, prominent defender of Israel - Campus Watch project to scrutinize Middle East studies at universities. Book acknowledges antisemitism appearing in rhetoric about Israel, but argues that accusations of antisemitism can sometimes be used to discourage legitimate criticism of Israeli government policy. Part 2: The Lobby in Action The Lobby Versus the Palestinians. Self heating meals The Shock Doctrine Naomi Klein (2007) Central argument Naomi Klein argues that governments and corporations exploit wars, coups, economic crises, and natural disasters to impose unpopular economic reforms. She calls this Disaster Capitalism : crises weaken opposition, enabling privatization, deregulation, austerity, and transfers of public wealth to private investors. The book traces this pattern from Augusto Pinochet 's Chile to post-Soviet Russia, the 1997 Asian Financial Crisis , the Iraq War , and Hurricane Katrina . Mechanisms and evidence 1. Chicago School economics and dictatorship Milton Friedman and the Chicago School of Economics advocated privatization, deregulation, and reduced government intervention. Following the 1973 Chilean Coup , Augusto Pinochet established a dictatorship and appointed Chicago-trained economists, the Chicago Boys , to implement market reforms. The regime suppressed unions and political opposition. Operation Condor coordinated repression across South American dictatorships. Klein argues that state violence weakened resistance to economic restructuring. 2. Thatcherism and the Falklands War Margaret Thatcher faced substantial opposition to privatization and restrictions on trade unions. Victory in the Falklands War (1982) strengthened her popularity and political authority. Her government subsequently accelerated privatization and defeated the British Miners' Strike (1984–1985). Klein argues that military victory facilitated previously unpopular domestic reforms. 3. Bolivia and shock therapy Bolivia's hyperinflation prompted President Víctor Paz Estenssoro to introduce Decree 21060 in 1985. Advised by Jeffrey Sachs , the government liberalized prices, restricted wages, and reduced public spending. Inflation fell sharply, but restructuring caused widespread hardship, particularly among miners. Klein argues that emergency stabilization enabled broader market reforms. 4. Poland, China, and South Africa After Poland's democratic transition, Leszek Balcerowicz introduced rapid price liberalization and privatization, departing from the worker-centered economic vision of parts of Solidarity . In China, Deng Xiaoping pursued market reforms while maintaining authoritarian rule. The government suppressed the Tiananmen Square Protests in 1989. In South Africa, the African National Congress achieved majority-rule democracy in 1994, but existing debt, property rights, and financial arrangements constrained economic redistribution. Klein argues that market liberalization does not necessarily produce democracy or economic equality. 5. Russian privatization Following the Soviet Union's collapse, Boris Yeltsin introduced rapid price liberalization and privatization amid severe economic hardship. During the 1993 Russian Constitutional Crisis , Yeltsin dissolved parliament and used military force against parliamentary opponents. The 1995 Loans-for-Shares program transferred stakes in valuable state enterprises to politically connected banks. Klein argues that privatization concentrated public wealth among Russian Oligarchs while weakening democratic oversight. 6. Asian financial crisis and IMF intervention The 1997 Asian Financial Crisis spread from Thailand to Indonesia, South Korea, and other economies. The International Monetary Fund attached austerity, financial restructuring, and market liberalization conditions to emergency loans. Foreign investors acquired distressed businesses at reduced prices. Klein argues that financial crises gave international lenders and investors leverage over domestic economic policy and ownership. 7. September 11 and privatized security Following the September 11 Attacks , the United States expanded military, intelligence, and counterterrorism spending. The Department of Homeland Security was established in 2002, creating extensive demand for private security and surveillance contractors. Companies including Halliburton and Blackwater benefited from expanded government contracting. Klein argues that privatization created businesses financially dependent on continued security spending. 8. Iraq's occupation and reconstruction Following the 2003 Invasion of Iraq , the Coalition Provisional Authority , led by Paul Bremer , reorganized Iraq's economy. CPA Order 39 permitted extensive foreign ownership and profit repatriation; CPA Order 12 suspended tariffs and trade restrictions. Halliburton and Bechtel received major reconstruction contracts amid widespread insecurity and infrastructure failures. Klein argues that the occupation imposed market reforms without Iraqi democratic consent while directing reconstruction spending toward foreign contractors. 9. Natural disasters and redevelopment After the 2004 Indian Ocean Tsunami , coastal restrictions in Sri Lanka prevented some fishing communities from rebuilding while tourism development expanded. Following Hurricane Katrina (2005), New Orleans reorganized public education around charter schools and demolished major public housing developments. Milton Friedman advocated using Katrina to introduce school-choice reforms. Klein argues that displacement weakened residents' ability to oppose changes to property rights and public institutions. 10. Israel and the security economy Klein describes Israel's growing security and technology industries alongside declining dependence on Palestinian labor. The Israeli West Bank Barrier and restrictions on Palestinian movement expanded security infrastructure while limiting Palestinian economic activity. She argues that profitable surveillance and military industries can reduce some economic incentives for ending prolonged conflict. Historical alternative During the Great Depression , Franklin D. Roosevelt introduced the New Deal , expanding public employment, regulation, and social protections. Klein contrasts this with crisis responses centered on privatization and austerity. Arguments challenged Market reforms require democratic consent: Chile, Russia, and Iraq demonstrate how reforms can proceed through authoritarian or externally imposed authority. Economic liberalization produces democracy: China expanded markets without political democratization. IMF rescue packages are politically neutral: Loan conditions can impose lasting changes to domestic economic policy. Privatization distributes economic power: Russia's transition concentrated public assets among politically connected investors. Private contractors improve government efficiency: Iraq's reconstruction revealed failures in accountability and service delivery. Disasters justify rebuilding institutions without residents' consent: Displaced communities retain claims to housing, property, and public services. Further questions Which Chilean economic reforms depended on authoritarian repression? Did IMF conditions improve or worsen recovery during the Asian financial crisis? Could Russia have privatized state enterprises without concentrating ownership among oligarchs? How did foreign contractors compare with Iraqi institutions in reconstruction outcomes? docs.text: Margaret Thatcher faced substantial opposition to privatization and restrictions on trade unions. Victory in the Falklands War (1982) strengthened her popularity and political authority. Her government subsequently accelerated privatization and defeated the British Miners' Strike (1984–1985). Klein argues that military victory facilitated previously unpopular domestic reforms.
docs.title: 2. Thatcherism and the Falklands War

docs.text: Bolivia's hyperinflation prompted President Víctor Paz Estenssoro to introduce Decree 21060 in 1985. Advised by Jeffrey Sachs , the government liberalized prices, restricted wages, and reduced public spending. Inflation fell sharply, but restructuring caused widespread hardship, particularly among miners. Klein argues that emergency stabilization enabled broader market reforms.
docs.title: 3. Bolivia and shock therapy

docs.text: After Poland's democratic transition, Leszek Balcerowicz introduced rapid price liberalization and privatization, departing from the worker-centered economic vision of parts of Solidarity . In China, Deng Xiaoping pursued market reforms while maintaining authoritarian rule. The government suppressed the Tiananmen Square Protests in 1989. In South Africa, the African National Congress achieved majority-rule democracy in 1994, but existing debt, property rights, and financial arrangements constrained economic redistribution. Klein argues that market liberalization does not necessarily produce democracy or economic equality.
docs.title: 4. Poland, China, and South Africa

docs.text: Following the Soviet Union's collapse, Boris Yeltsin introduced rapid price liberalization and privatization amid severe economic hardship. During the 1993 Russian Constitutional Crisis , Yeltsin dissolved parliament and used military force against parliamentary opponents. The 1995 Loans-for-Shares program transferred stakes in valuable state enterprises to politically connected banks. Klein argues that privatization concentrated public wealth among Russian Oligarchs while weakening democratic oversight.
docs.title: 5. Russian privatization

docs.text: The 1997 Asian Financial Crisis spread from Thailand to Indonesia, South Korea, and other economies. The International Monetary Fund attached austerity, financial restructuring, and market liberalization conditions to emergency loans. Foreign investors acquired distressed businesses at reduced prices. Klein argues that financial crises gave international lenders and investors leverage over domestic economic policy and ownership.
docs.title: 6. Asian financial crisis and IMF intervention

docs.text: Following the September 11 Attacks , the United States expanded military, intelligence, and counterterrorism spending. The Department of Homeland Security was established in 2002, creating extensive demand for private security and surveillance contractors. Companies including Halliburton and Blackwater benefited from expanded government contracting. Klein argues that privatization created businesses financially dependent on continued security spending.
docs.title: 7. September 11 and privatized security

docs.text: Following the 2003 Invasion of Iraq , the Coalition Provisional Authority , led by Paul Bremer , reorganized Iraq's economy. CPA Order 39 permitted extensive foreign ownership and profit repatriation; CPA Order 12 suspended tariffs and trade restrictions. Halliburton and Bechtel received major reconstruction contracts amid widespread insecurity and infrastructure failures. Klein argues that the occupation imposed market reforms without Iraqi democratic consent while directing reconstruction spending toward foreign contractors.
docs.title: 8. Iraq's occupation and reconstruction

docs.text: After the 2004 Indian Ocean Tsunami , coastal restrictions in Sri Lanka prevented some fishing communities from rebuilding while tourism development expanded. Following Hurricane Katrina (2005), New Orleans reorganized public education around charter schools and demolished major public housing developments. Milton Friedman advocated using Katrina to introduce school-choice reforms. Klein argues that displacement weakened residents' ability to oppose changes to property rights and public institutions.
docs.title: 9. Natural disasters and redevelopment

docs.text: Klein describes Israel's growing security and technology industries alongside declining dependence on Palestinian labor. The Israeli West Bank Barrier and restrictions on Palestinian movement expanded security infrastructure while limiting Palestinian economic activity. She argues that profitable surveillance and military industries can reduce some economic incentives for ending prolonged conflict.
docs.title: 10. Israel and the security economy

docs.text: During the Great Depression , Franklin D. Roosevelt introduced the New Deal , expanding public employment, regulation, and social protections. Klein contrasts this with crisis responses centered on privatization and austerity.
docs.title: Historical alternative

docs.text: Market reforms require democratic consent: Chile, Russia, and Iraq demonstrate how reforms can proceed through authoritarian or externally imposed authority. Economic liberalization produces democracy: China expanded markets without political democratization. IMF rescue packages are politically neutral: Loan conditions can impose lasting changes to domestic economic policy. Privatization distributes economic power: Russia's transition concentrated public assets among politically connected investors. Private contractors improve government efficiency: Iraq's reconstruction revealed failures in accountability and service delivery. Disasters justify rebuilding institutions without residents' consent: Displaced communities retain claims to housing, property, and public services.

docs.text: White Trash Nancy Isenberg (2016) Central argument American class hierarchy predates independence. British colonization relied on transporting the poor as disposable labor, while colonial landownership, inheritance, and political institutions concentrated wealth. The American Revolution replaced hereditary aristocracy with republican ideals but did not eliminate inherited economic inequality. Isenberg traces how elites repeatedly portrayed poor whites as lazy, uncivilized, or biologically inferior to justify their exclusion. Frontier expansion, slavery, eugenics, New Deal reform, and modern political culture changed the language of class without eliminating its structural foundations. The myth of universal upward mobility obscured the importance of inherited property and political power. Mechanisms and evidence 1. Colonization and disposable labor English promoters including Richard Hakluyt advocated sending vagrants, convicts, and the unemployed to America. Colonies would remove supposedly unproductive people from England while supplying cheap labor and imperial wealth. In Jamestown , indentured servants exchanged years of labor for passage. High mortality, harsh discipline, and manipulated contracts undermined promises of eventual independence. The Headright System awarded Virginia land for importing laborers, allowing wealthy sponsors to accumulate acreage while servants remained dependent. 2. Landownership and colonial hierarchy John Locke helped draft the 1669 Fundamental Constitutions of Carolina , which proposed hereditary ranks of landgraves and caciques, large estates, and hereditary servitude. William Byrd II portrayed North Carolina's landless squatters as idle and uncivilized. His 1728 boundary survey exposed the contempt of Virginia's landed elite toward poorer settlers. James Oglethorpe founded Georgia as a colony intended to rehabilitate Britain's poor through agricultural labor. Restrictions on slavery and large landholdings faced planter opposition; Georgia legalized slavery in 1751. 3. Republican equality and inherited class Benjamin Franklin promoted industriousness, marriage, and population growth as foundations of colonial prosperity, while treating idleness and dependency as social threats. Thomas Jefferson celebrated independent farmers but proposed selecting talented children from poorer families for public education, leaving most of the class hierarchy intact. Jefferson's Notes on the State of Virginia linked cultivation, environment, and human improvement. His ideas about breeding and racial inheritance contradicted his egalitarian political language. 4. Frontier expansion and Jacksonian democracy Western squatters occupied Indigenous territory before formal land sales. Speculators and wealthy purchasers frequently acquired the best land, displacing poorer settlers. Andrew Jackson cultivated an image as a frontier common man despite his plantation wealth and slaveholding. His political rise helped transform the backwoodsman into a democratic symbol. The Indian Removal Act of 1830 facilitated white settlement and land speculation while forcibly dispossessing Native nations. Expansion did not guarantee equal access to property. 5. Slavery and the poor white class Southern elites used labels such as crackers , clay-eaters , and poor white trash to distinguish landless whites from respectable slaveholding families. Hinton Rowan Helper argued in The Impending Crisis of the South (1857) that slavery impoverished nonslaveholding whites by concentrating land, labor, and political influence among planters. James Henry Hammond defended slavery through his 1858 Mudsill Theory , claiming every society required a permanent laboring class. During the American Civil War , Confederate conscription exemptions for men supervising twenty or more enslaved people intensified resentment over wealthy slaveholders' privileges. 6. Eugenics and hereditary poverty After the Civil War, elite commentators increasingly described poor whites through inherited degeneracy, defective bloodlines, and supposedly inferior reproduction. Francis Galton 's eugenic theories influenced American reformers who treated poverty, disability, and criminality as hereditary problems. In Buck v. Bell (1927), the Supreme Court upheld Virginia's compulsory sterilization law. Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr. endorsed preventing people classified as genetically unfit from reproducing. Carrie Buck , a poor Virginia woman, became the test case for state control over reproduction, demonstrating how class prejudice acquired medical and legal authority. 7. The Great Depression and government reform The Great Depression exposed widespread tenant farming, landlessness, and rural poverty, challenging claims that hard work guaranteed independence. Rexford Tugwell and the Resettlement Administration pursued planned communities and agricultural resettlement to address structural poverty rather than individual moral failure. Franklin D. Roosevelt 's New Deal challenged older assumptions about government responsibility, but agricultural reform faced resistance from landlords and entrenched local elites. Sociologist Howard W. Odum investigated the category of poor whites, documenting how regional stereotypes combined economic circumstances with judgments about character and ancestry. 8. Postwar prosperity and the country-boy image Postwar homeownership and consumer prosperity reinforced the ideal of a universal middle class, even as trailer residents faced exclusion through zoning and local housing restrictions. Elvis Presley transformed working-class southern identity into commercially successful popular culture. Rural origins became marketable without eliminating class stigma. Orval Faubus and George Wallace used rural populist identities and resistance to desegregation to mobilize white voters. Lyndon B. Johnson drew on his impoverished Texas Hill Country background to promote the War on Poverty , while confronting opposition to federal intervention. 9. Redneck identity as entertainment and politics Deliverance (1972) portrayed Appalachian backwoods residents through violence and degeneracy, reviving older stereotypes of isolated rural populations. Jimmy Carter 's presidential image emphasized rural authenticity, while his brother Billy Carter became a national caricature of the southern redneck. Dolly Parton , NASCAR, and White Trash Cooking (1986) helped turn stigmatized working-class imagery into entertainment and consumer identity. Bill Clinton 's Arkansas upbringing became a recurring explanation for his ambition and sexual behavior. Comparisons with Thomas Jefferson revealed persistent assumptions about breeding and respectability. Sarah Palin 's 2008 vice-presidential campaign revived the country-outsider identity, presenting rural authenticity as a political qualification while attracting class-based ridicule.

docs.text: Obsidian Bases Workflow Read the existing .base file before editing it. Define global scope with filters . Add computed values under formulas only when needed. Configure property display names and one or more views. Validate YAML, formula references, quoting, and date/duration operations. Open or query the Base in Obsidian when the CLI is available. Schema filters: and: - 'file.ext == "md"' - 'status != "archived"' formulas: days_until_due: 'if(due, (date(due) - today()).days.round(), "")' properties: status: displayName: Status formula.days_until_due: displayName: "Days Until Due" summaries: mean_rounded: 'values.mean().round(2)' views: - type: table name: Active limit: 50 filters: and: - 'status != "done"' order: - file.name - status - due - formula.days_until_due sort: - property: due direction: ASC groupBy: property: status direction: ASC summaries: formula.days_until_due: Average Views may be table , cards , or list . A map view depends on compatible map support. order sets which properties a view shows; sort sets row order, one property / direction entry per key, applied in turn. Obsidian sorts only by properties that are also listed in order , so include every sort property there. Filters and properties Filters may be a single expression or recursively nested and , or , and not objects. Property namespaces are: note properties: status or note.status file metadata: file.name , file.path , file.folder , file.ctime , file.mtime , file.tags , file.links , and file.backlinks formulas: formula.days_until_due Use file.hasTag() , file.hasLink() , file.hasProperty() , and file.inFolder() for indexed file relationships. The this value refers to the Base itself, the embedding note, or the active file depending on where the Base is rendered. Formula rules Guard optional properties with if() . Date subtraction returns a Duration, not a number. Access .days , .hours , or another numeric field before calling number methods such as .round() . Round day counts: across a daylight-saving change .days can be fractional. Every formula.X used by a view or property configuration must have a matching X entry under formulas . Wrap formulas containing double quotes in YAML single quotes. Quote YAML strings containing special characters, especially colons and leading punctuation. Read Functions reference for function and type-specific operations, and Examples for complete task-tracker and daily-notes Bases. Validation checklist The document parses as YAML and has a views list. View order , groupBy , and summaries reference defined note, file, or formula properties. Formula quoting is balanced and duration math accesses a numeric field. Every sort property also appears in that view's order .
